sense: a guest who calls or stays

terms.grammar: noun, third declension; feminine hospita, hospitae
evidence: Ov. F. 5.502: hospitibus jānua nostra patet
terms.comment: A guest who comes to the house, to call or to stay; at the table he is a convīva (see guest). The same word is the host (see host): the sentence shows which is meant.

terms.gloss: a caller who comes to pay his respects
terms.comment: The Roman morning caller at a great man’s house, and later a courtier (Lewis & Short): a visit of courtesy, not a friend dropping in.

phrases.latin: sī vespertīnus subitō tē oppresserit hospes
phrases.english: if a visitor descends on you suddenly in the evening
and our door is open to visitors

phrases.latin: hospes, hīc bene manēbis, hīc summum bonum voluptās est
phrases.english: guest, you will be well off staying here; here the highest good is pleasure

phrases.latin: Vīn' ad tē ad cēnam veniam? — Sī possim, velim; vērum hīc apud mē cēnant aliēnī novem.
phrases.english: Shall I come to yours for dinner? — I’d like that, if I could; but I’ve got nine people from outside dining with me here.

phrases.latin: hospite ventūrō cessābit nēmo tuōrum. ‘verre pavīmentum, nitidās ostende columnās, ārida cum tōtā dēscendat arānea tēlā, hic lēve argentum, vāsa aspera tergeat alter.’
phrases.english: when a guest is coming, none of your household will sit idle: “Sweep the floor, make the columns shine, get every dry spider down with its web; one of you polish the smooth silver, another the embossed cups.”

phrases.latin: Stella, Nepōs, Canī, Ceriālis, Flacce, venītis? septem sigma capit, sex sumus, adde Lupum.
phrases.english: Stella, Nepos, Canius, Cerialis, Flaccus, are you coming? The couch takes seven; we are six; add Lupus.

phrases.latin: Hodiē hospitēs ad nōs veniunt: age, adjuvā mē pavīmentum verrere.
phrases.english: We’re having guests today: come on, help me sweep the floor.

sources: Lewis & Short: hospes · Lewis & Short: salutator
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 402.
